title: How computers store numbers
text:
Hi everyone, welcome back to the channel. If you're new here, I make videos about how computers actually work under the hood, and today's one is a question I get asked a lot in the comments. Before we start, huge thanks to everyone who supported the channel this month, it really helps.

So, how does a computer store a number? You might imagine there are tiny digits written somewhere inside the chip, but there aren't. A computer is built from billions of tiny switches called transistors, and each switch can only be off or on. We write off as zero and on as one. One of these zeros or ones is called a bit, which is short for binary digit.

When I was a kid I had one of those light-up toys with a row of eight bulbs, and I didn't know it then but it was basically a byte. Anyway.

Because each bit only has two states, computers count in base two, which we call binary. In our normal decimal system each place is worth ten times the one to its right: ones, tens, hundreds. In binary each place is worth two times the one to its right: ones, twos, fours, eights, sixteens and so on. So the binary number one zero one means one four, no twos and one one, which is five.

Eight bits grouped together make a byte. A single byte can represent two to the power eight, which is two hundred and fifty-six, different values, so it can store any whole number from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. That's why you see the number two fifty-five all over the place in computing, for example in colour codes, where each of red, green and blue gets one byte.

What about bigger numbers? We just use more bytes. Four bytes, which is thirty-two bits, can store over four billion different values. Sixty-four bits can store numbers so large you'd never count to them in your lifetime.

Okay, but what about negative numbers? This is where it gets clever. Most computers use a method called two's complement. In two's complement the leftmost bit acts as the sign, and to make a number negative you flip all the bits and add one. The nice thing is that the computer can then add and subtract positive and negative numbers with exactly the same circuit, which keeps the hardware simple.

And text? Text is stored as numbers too. Every character is given a code. In the old ASCII standard the capital letter A is sixty-five. Today we use Unicode, which gives a code to characters from almost every writing system in the world, including Hindi, Tamil, Chinese and even emoji, and an encoding called UTF-8 turns those codes into bytes.

Fractions, like three point one four, are stored using floating point, which works a bit like scientific notation: some bits store the digits and some store where the decimal point goes. That's also why if you type point one plus point two in many programming languages you get point three zero zero zero zero something, because some decimal fractions can't be stored exactly in binary.

So to sum up: switches, bits, binary place values, bytes, and clever encodings for negatives, text and fractions. If you enjoyed this, you know what to do, and I'll see you in the next one.
keyPoints: Computers are built from transistors that act as switches, each either off or on, written as zero or one, called a bit.
Computers count in binary, base two, where each place is worth twice the place to its right.
Eight bits make a byte, which can store 256 values, from 0 to 255.
Negative numbers are stored with two's complement: flip all the bits and add one.
Text is stored as numbers using character codes such as ASCII and Unicode with UTF-8.
Fractions are stored as floating point, so some decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly.
